Family

Does birth order shape personality?

The responsible eldest, the overlooked middle child, the rebellious youngest… Large studies find barely any differences.

It is one of the most widespread beliefs about families: firstborns are responsible and ambitious; middle children diplomatic and somewhat overlooked; and the youngest charming and rebellious. The idea goes back to the psychoanalyst Alfred Adler, who in the early 20th century gave great importance to each child's position.

What large studies found

In 2015, Julia Rohrer, Boris Egloff and Stefan Schmukle analysed data from more than 20,000 people in Germany, the UK and the US, also comparing siblings within the same family. They found no differences in extraversion, emotional stability, agreeableness, conscientiousness or imagination by birth order. That same year, another study of nearly 400,000 US high-school students reached a similar conclusion: the differences were minimal.

The only consistent finding was a small advantage on intelligence tests for older siblings, about one and a half points on average: imperceptible in daily life.

What might matter

Although birth order barely affects personality, large studies do find a small advantage for firstborns on intelligence tests, of about one or two IQ points compared with the next sibling. A study of almost 250,000 Norwegian conscripts found that what mattered was the order in which each child was raised, not biological order: second-born children whose older sibling had died young scored like firstborns. The difference is too small to notice in everyday life.

What about only children?

There is a stereotype that only children are spoiled, selfish or unsociable. Toni Falbo and Denise Polit's classic review of more than a hundred studies found that they did not differ from children with siblings in sociability or adjustment, and even had a slight advantage in academic achievement and in their relationship with their parents.

Why do we keep believing it?

Because we compare siblings of different ages: the eldest seems more responsible because they are older. And because we remember the cases that fit the stereotype. Personality depends on many factors, and birth order weighs very little.

References

  1. Rohrer, J. M., Egloff, B. y Schmukle, S. C. (2015). Examining the effects of birth order on personality. PNAS, 112(46), 14224–14229.
  2. Damian, R. I. y Roberts, B. W. (2015). The associations of birth order with personality and intelligence in a representative sample of U.S. high school students. Journal of Research in Personality, 58, 96–105.
  3. Kristensen, P. y Bjerkedal, T. (2007). Explaining the relation between birth order and intelligence. Science, 316, 1717.
  4. Falbo, T. y Polit, D. F. (1986). Quantitative review of the only child literature. Psychological Bulletin, 100(2), 176–189.
